memories.memory_text: I said goodbye to Micah Davenport and Rowan Hayes, telling them I'd see them again in the spring.

grounded_facts: Graham York and Micah Davenport share a meaningful, wordless look as Graham York departs, suggesting unresolved feelings or emotional significance.
memories.memory_text: I shared a final look with Micah Davenport as I left—she watched me go, and it felt like time slowed down, heavy with things we didn’t say.

grounded_facts: The characters leave the Pinecrest Park, marking the end of an era and their emotional farewell to the old life and Pinecrest Park.
A collective gathering and emotional parting at the Pinecrest Park, where characters say goodbye to Pinecrest Park and each other.
memories.memory_text: I stood with Micah Davenport and Rowan Hayes as we all prepared to leave the Pinecrest Park, and I said, 'Until the spring, then. Goodbye my friends, until we meet again!'—knowing this was more than a farewell, it was the end of an era for all of us and our lives tied to Pinecrest Park.

grounded_facts: Jamie Brooks checks on Graham York's physical condition after his injury.
memories.memory_text: I remember Jamie Brooks asking me about my leg, and I told him it was fine before telling him to go.

grounded_facts: Graham York exits Maplewood House through the back door and gets into the the silver letter, indicating a transition in location and the start of a journey.
memories.memory_text: I exited through the back door of Maplewood House and got into the the silver letter, sitting in the back as we started to leave.

grounded_facts: Graham York demands the the silver letter to stop multiple times, escalating his tone until Skyler Vaughn complies, then exits the vehicle.
Graham York forcefully tells Skyler Vaughn to stop the the silver letter, overriding Skyler Vaughn's initial refusal.
memories.memory_text: I demanded Skyler Vaughn stop the the silver letter, raising my voice until he finally did, and then I got out—I had to get back to Maplewood House no matter what.

grounded_facts: Jamie Brooks expresses shock and confusion at Graham York's decision to leave the the silver letter.
memories.memory_text: I heard Jamie Brooks shout my name and ask what I was doing, clearly shocked and confused when I decided to leave the the silver letter.

grounded_facts: Graham York exits the moving vehicle and begins running back toward Maplewood House, separating from Jamie Brooks and Skyler Vaughn.
memories.memory_text: I got out of the the silver letter after Skyler Vaughn stopped it, and I started running back toward Maplewood House, knowing I had to get there no matter what.

grounded_facts: Graham York, as Graham York, returns to the stage after deciding not to board the train, creating a pivotal emotional confrontation with Micah Davenport.
memories.memory_text: I had to come back — I couldn't board the train. The moment I stepped onto the platform, the blood drained from my heart, and I knew I couldn't leave without seeing her.

grounded_facts: Graham York grabs Micah Davenport during their argument, intensifying the physical and emotional stakes.
memories.memory_text: I grabbed Micah Davenport during our argument, trying to make her listen to me despite the tension between us.

grounded_facts: In emotional distress, Micah Davenport kicks Graham York, expressing defiance and resistance.
memories.memory_text: I saw her kick out at me in emotional distress, resisting what I was saying, but I stayed firm even though it hurt.

grounded_facts: Graham York declares his love for Micah Davenport, asserting that his motivations have never been about the leather watch but about emotion.
memories.memory_text: I declared my love for Micah Davenport, telling her it's never been about the leather watch—that she knows it's about emotion, and that she's afraid because I love her.

grounded_facts: Graham York physically blocks Micah Davenport from leaving the stage, escalating tension and forcing confrontation.
memories.memory_text: I blocked her from leaving the stage, and when she tried to get past me, I held my ground — I had to make her listen, even as she broke away from me.

grounded_facts: Graham York repeatedly urges Micah Davenport to meet him in Moscow, framing it as a chance for emotional connection and change.
memories.memory_text: I kept urging her to meet me in Moscow, hoping it could be our chance to finally connect and make things right between us.

grounded_facts: Micah Davenport observes that Graham York is bleeding, drawing attention to his physical vulnerability and the cost of his return.
memories.memory_text: I noticed Micah Davenport saw that I was bleeding and called it out, making my injury real to everyone.

grounded_facts: A live theatrical performance in which actors portray characters in an emotionally charged scene involving return, confession, and confrontation.
memories.memory_text: I remember the weight of the moment, the tension in the air like a live wire — Pinecrest Park destroyed behind us, and as the lights faded, white cherry blossoms appeared, marking the end of something.

grounded_facts: Noel Keller cues a lighting change that marks the emotional climax, shifting focus to silhouette and symbolism as the scene concludes.
memories.memory_text: I think Noel Keller cued the lights to fade slowly, shifting everything into shadow and symbolism as the scene ended, though I wasn't sure exactly what it meant at the time.

memories.memory_text: I straightened up when the the silver letter approached, opened the window, but it just went to the EZ-PASS lane—didn’t even slow down for me. I closed the window and watched it go, then drank the last of the coffee.
She asked if it was time for us, and I just stopped eating—my fork froze halfway to my mouth.
She looked at me and asked if I still loved her, and I felt like I couldn't move—then the doorbell rang, and I got up.

I sat there while the detective paced, his voice pressing me to speak, but I said nothing—even when he mentioned my wife, my job. When I finally looked up, meeting his eyes, I felt the weight of what I was choosing, though I wasn’t sure if it was courage or fear.

I stood there in my suit, blinking when the gavel came down—four years. My lawyer patted me on the back like it was a win, but all I could see was Terry Marlowe just sitting there, staring at me without moving.
Jamie Brooks gripped my arm and said this was a crossroads, that I’d have to fight for my dream—then right after, something cracked against my head.
I got up and charged them, swinging wildly, feeling my fists hit bodies—but then they were all over me, beating me down even as I kept fighting.

I remember sitting across from Terry Marlowe, seeing her dressed up, trying to smile, and then hearing her say, 'I fell in love.' I felt the weight of those words settle in, and I just said, 'Oh. Okay. Wow...' like I had time to process, but I didn't.
Jamie Brooks sat down beside me, put his hand on my shoulder, and told me he’d been almost married—turned down because he was too short. I said, 'Books and covers,' and he agreed.
I stood by the door, bag in hand, and told Jamie Brooks I was going to miss him—my voice was quiet, but I meant it.
Jamie Brooks told me 'your dream is your myth is your truth,' and I corrected him—just like old times—before walking out for good.

I stood at the door of my old house, hesitated, then rang the bell—when it opened, Skyler Vaughn was there, wearing a suit, like he belonged, and called out to Terry Marlowe like he was the one who’d built this life.
I asked Terry Marlowe if she was happy, and she said she was. I meant it when I told her I was glad.
Skyler Vaughn thanked me for not giving up his name. I said I didn't know his name. He said it was Skyler Vaughn. I said 'you're welcome, Skyler Vaughn.'
I stepped into the field with the shovel in hand, rain soaking through my clothes, and began digging into the wet earth while the old man stood back with his wheelbarrow, just watching.
I dug another ditch in the snow, the cold biting through my gloves, while the Sage Dalton stood there watching, motionless.
I said 'Good,' but I couldn't speak when she asked what was next—I just felt the weight of my boots on the floor, waiting for something I couldn't name.

I was urinating when I saw the old newspaper photo on the wall—cops standing in front of the Buffalo Westhaven Plaza with crates of booze, and then another one in a tunnel with a hole above him. The moment I read 'TUNNEL DISCOVERED,' I stopped peeing, staring at it, something clicking in my head.
I told Jamie Brooks, 'I did the time, I may as well have done the crime'—the words felt heavy, like I was finally making sense of the years I lost.
I leaned in and whispered that I needed his help to rob the Westhaven Plaza—the one I didn’t rob—and for a moment, I believed he might actually say yes.

I stood in the back of Maplewood House and saw her on stage—Micah Davenport—speaking through tears about loving her country, and I couldn't look away. She was good, really good, and for the first time I didn't just see the woman who hit me, but someone... else.

I saw the play poster behind her and said it looked funny—actors on a tree. Then she explained it was the director’s way of mocking American culture, how we treat identity like fruit to be consumed. That stuck with me.

She said it was her last play in Buffalo, just like Bennett Foster’s the brass lantern was his final one. I remember asking if she was leaving, and then she finished her coffee and walked away. I watched her go past the Westhaven Plaza.

I told Jamie Brooks I knew he could do it, and that I was there to pick him up—no the silver letter, just me. He looked so lost, asking where the the silver letter was, like I’d failed him just by showing up on foot.
He started pounding on the gates, trying to go back inside. I put my arm around him when he couldn't breathe—felt him shaking—and said we’d miss the bus, just to keep him moving forward.

I pointed to the tunnel in the old photo and told Jamie Brooks it was a start, that it was an article—not just a cartoon—because I needed him to see it wasn't nothing. I said no guns, because someone could get hurt, and I meant it.
I stood on the stage after Jamie Brooks left, feeling the quiet, and asked Micah Davenport if it was fun pretending to be other people—then realized she wasn't pretending at all, not really.

I told Micah Davenport I just got out of Westhaven Theater, and for a moment I wasn't sure how she'd react—she froze, then laughed, then said I looked like a criminal, and it hit me how this truth changes things.
I saw her through the glass, smiling and touching her belly, so peaceful—like she had a life I wasn’t part of anymore. I stepped back and let the doors close.
I threw down my shovel and told Jamie Brooks I wasn't leaving her—he didn't understand, but I couldn't keep digging like it didn't matter.
I told her to meet me in California, that we had to do it tonight — the only time we could get into the small lantern — and I stepped closer, telling her I wanted us to be together.
She laughed when I said I wanted us to be together, then told me we only screwed a couple of times — that it meant nothing — and called me a thief, told me to go rob my Westhaven Plaza.

Good God in Heaven. My father was one of your father's serfs, and your grandfather's serf before that. But you, you did so much for me in the old days that I've forgotten all that...
This is not a home. This is a Westhaven Theater.
I used to sit in that toll booth and think about just getting in one of those cars, going wherever they went. Just joining someone else's life.
Even more beautiful, and dressed like a Parisian...you could blow me down.

relations.relation_summary: Graham York and Micah Davenport share a complex, evolving relationship marked by deep romantic involvement, professional collaboration, and emotional turbulence. Social relationship evidence reveals a strong romantic and intimate connection, with multiple instances of affectionate dialogue, physical intimacy (including kissing and implied sexual history), and emotional vulnerability, particularly during reflective moments such as their conversation near Niagara Falls, where they discuss life, death, and personal risk. Their bond is further reinforced by mutual intellectual engagement, as seen in their collaborative discussions about acting, self-representation, and Bennett Foster’s the brass lantern, indicating both emotional and artistic compatibility. They are also co-conspirators in a Westhaven Plaza heist, working together on a plan involving the small lantern and a tunnel, which underscores a level of trust and shared purpose beyond romance. However, the relationship is fraught with conflict and instability. Micah Davenport explicitly rejects Graham York multiple times, stating the relationship 'isn't going to work out,' accusing him of being a thief, and demanding he leave, which causes Graham York visible emotional distress. These confrontations reveal a power struggle and diverging life goals—Micah Davenport seeks a future in Hollywood, while Graham York remains entangled in criminal behavior. Key events such as Micah Davenport checking on Graham York after his injury, offering him water, and attempting to call an ambulance demonstrate enduring care despite the hostility. Their shared moments—watching Niagara Falls, sitting beneath the Hollywood sign, laughing in the sun—contrast sharply with scenes of separation and accusation, illustrating a push-pull dynamic driven by longing, disillusionment, and unresolved attachment. The relationship evolves from romantic pursuit to intimate partnership, then to collaboration in crime and art, and ultimately to emotional rupture, though residual affection and understanding persist. This evolution significantly impacts both characters’ decisions, including Graham York’s criminal actions and Micah Davenport’s hesitation to fully sever ties.

Graham York and Jamie Brooks share a complex, evolving relationship defined by both deep collaboration and moments of tension. Social relationship evidence reveals a strong mentor-mentee dynamic, with Jamie Brooks frequently addressing Graham York as 'kid' and offering philosophical guidance about life, dreams, and personal purpose—encouraging him to 'fight for that dream' and embrace his role as Evan Hart. This paternalistic influence is balanced by their shared identity as partners in crime, as they repeatedly plan and execute a Westhaven Plaza robbery using a hidden tunnel, demonstrating mutual trust and strategic cooperation. Their affinity is reinforced through multiple collaborative events, such as discussing the heist in whispers, moving the armoire to access the tunnel, walking into the banking hall, and packing their apartment together—actions that signify both operational coordination and emotional companionship. Graham York comforts Jamie Brooks physically and emotionally after his release from Westhaven Theater, while Jamie Brooks supports Graham York during moments of doubt, indicating reciprocal emotional support. However, the relationship is not without conflict: Jamie Brooks expresses hostility when Graham York reveals their plans, calling it 'not kosher,' and later states, 'I hope I never see you again,' suggesting ruptures in trust. memories.memory_text: I yelled at him—'What the fuck are you doing?'—like it was his fault, even though I was the one who hit him. I was on the phone, yeah, but I know how to drive.
Blair Sawyer told me to park the the silver letter, so I did—pulled it over fast. I didn’t argue, just followed what he said while he helped Graham York limp away.
I told him rehearsal is all pain, and he just stood there like he wanted to understand, but what’s there to get?
He opened the cafe door and said his name like it meant something—Graham York—and I just said mine, Micah Davenport, like handing over a ticket.

I told Graham York about the director’s joke—actors’ faces as falling fruit, a comment on how American culture chews up identity. I even quoted that line about the American dream becoming the world’s nightmare, though I wasn’t sure I believed it.

I admitted I wasn’t really listening to the director—I was just playing it safe. Then I told Graham York this is my last play here in Buffalo. I didn’t say why, but I felt it—the finality—when I said it.

I screamed so loud after that awful rehearsal, punching the air like it was going to fix anything. Then the door slammed into someone—Graham York—and I just snapped, 'Goddamn Czech Bennett Foster shit!'

Jamie Brooks said Bennett Foster was his favorite Russian besides Gorbachev, and I actually laughed—couldn't help it. Then he asked to come inside, and I just said yes, even though I didn't know him from a hole in the wall.

I told Graham York that acting isn't about pretending to be someone else—it's about finding a part of myself and revealing it through a character. When he said I was still playing 'me,' I just said, 'Yes. Exactly. In a way.'

I was eating my sandwich, just trying to make small talk, and then he says he just got out of Westhaven Theater—like it’s nothing. I laughed at first, but when I looked at him, really looked, I said, 'Yeah,' and meant it. He’s a criminal.
I told Graham York what the play really means—how it’s about being forced to let go of the past just to survive. It came out clearer than I meant it to, like I was talking about myself.

He asked me to dinner—Golden Dragon, eight o’clock. I said sure, even though I don’t do things like that. Then he said ‘see you,’ and I told him to stay out of Westhaven Theater, like a joke, but my voice was quiet.
I told Graham York I don't just want to be good—I want to be great, and not in Buffalo. I said it out loud: Hollywood. Before it's too late.

I remember staring down at the falls, the water roaring below, and thinking about all those bodies caught in the current—how they took the risk and ended up the same as they were in life. Nothing changes, not even death.

I laughed—actually laughed—when Graham York said he was going to rob the same Westhaven Plaza he got arrested for trying to rob by mistake. 'You're fucking hilarious, Graham York,' I said, and meant it, even if I didn't know why.
I handed Graham York the script and told him to read Evan Hart’s lines like he meant them, like it was real—like he was saying it to me, not just reading words on a page.
After he read the line about wanting my eyes to look at him like before, I stepped closer and said, 'I'm glad I ran you over,' then we kissed—just like that.

I opened my eyes and saw him there, already looking back at me like he knew I was waking up. I said 'Good morning,' then climbed on top of him—felt the weight of it, the closeness, and didn’t pull away.
I called Graham York a greedy little criminal after he avoided saying why he’d risk going back to Westhaven Theater — the way he just smiled told me he knew exactly what I was digging for.
When he quoted Bennett Foster like that—'I just want you to believe in me'—I actually felt something; I said he was good, and I meant it, even if I didn’t want to.
I stood on stage and shouted that I wanted to be free of the stone weighing me down, like I could finally say out loud what I’ve been carrying for years.
I saw my mother’s image float across the screen in a white dress, and I laughed—really laughed—like for a second, she was really there.

Jamie Brooks got into my the silver letter and said Graham York should play Evan Hart—like it was some kind of cosmic joke, like Graham York wasn’t just a man from my past but suddenly a character in one of my plays.
I slapped Jamie Brooks across the face after realizing he’d set this up—pushed Graham York into the role like it was inevitable, like my feelings didn’t matter at all.
I whispered 'Show me, tell me' to Graham York—just barely loud enough for him to hear—like I was asking him to prove something, not just act it.
After Graham York finished, he looked at me and I looked back—just for a second—and in that moment I knew he’d really done it, not just performed, but *become* it.
I asked Graham York if this makes me an accessory, and he just said yes—like it was that simple. I couldn’t tell if I was helping him or getting dragged into something worse.

I remember asking Graham York why he was really robbing the Westhaven Plaza, and seeing him hesitate before admitting it wasn't about the the leather watch—it was about finally doing something, after years of just going along.
I remember pouring honey into my tea, turning to him after he asked if I was okay, and saying, 'Not for a girl like me, Graham York'—like it was obvious, like I had to remind him who I was.

I shut off the TV when my Buffalotto commercial came on—he said he liked it, but I couldn’t stand watching myself like that. When Graham York suggested meeting out west, I laughed, then told him I wasn’t going anywhere. Plans change.
I told Graham York this wasn't going to work out, and when he looked at me like he didn't already know, I said I did — I'd known all along. Then I told him to leave, and he just stood there, stunned.

I saw him sitting there in that stupid beard, watching me like nothing had changed. I told him I came to my senses — and that he should too — then kept walking. When he followed, I just said, 'I don't want to, Graham York.'

I was finishing my makeup when Graham York showed up, talking about meeting him in California and pulling off the heist that night—like none of it mattered. I told him straight: we screwed a couple of times, so what? I don’t want to be with you. You’re a thief. Go rob your Westhaven Plaza.

I walked into the nursery and felt a rush of old feeling—my voice cracked saying it was my childhood room—and then I saw Graham York waiting, expecting something, but I just kept walking and kissed everyone except him.

I remember standing on the stage, speaking those words about my childhood—how I used to sleep in the nursery and wake up happy, looking out at the garden. When I said 'Oh, my the brass lantern,' I could see it in my mind, not as it was, but as it is now—withered, fading, like everything else.
I watched Graham York walk away, and for a moment it felt like he was moving through water—slow, distant, already gone. We didn’t speak, but that look… it said everything we never could.

memories.memory_text: I extended my hand and told the new guy, 'I'm Jamie Brooks,' after he said he was in for a Westhaven Plaza job he didn't commit—same old story, mistaken identity.
I told him 'Life' when he asked my charge, then added, 'Don't worry, you'll get used to it,' after seeing the look on his face.
I told Graham York his dream is his truth is his destiny—like it was some law of the universe, like he had to hear it before everything went sideways.
I saw the guys coming, pulled Graham York close, and told him this was his moment—then watched him charge in like he actually believed it.
I remember pounding on the Westhaven Theater gates, shouting for Dave and Carl to let me back in—I didn't want to be out here, it didn't feel right.
I couldn't catch my breath, just kept gasping—I was sure I was going to die right there on the pavement, and I told Graham York so.

I sat down on the small bed in Graham York's living room after he showed me the books—'Future Shock' and Dostoyevsky—like they were mine now. I said thanks, and when he asked if I needed anything else, I just nodded and said yeah.

I stared at that old photo in the bathroom, the one from the Prohibition era, and couldn't believe Graham York was serious—like some cartoon in a pissoir was a real plan. I called him out, asking if he was dreaming, because a tunnel from eighty years ago? That's ridiculous.

After pushing back, I finally said yes—let's go look at the Westhaven Plaza. I told Graham York at least we know the Westhaven Plaza's still there, marking the first real step toward doing this thing, even if the tunnel's a long shot.
I asked Tuttle if the small lantern was still in the same spot, and when he said 'since 1891' and confirmed it hadn't moved, I knew the tunnel would work.
I told Micah Davenport I used to perform here—right there in the alley, with Graham York giving me that look—then played it cool, name-dropped Bennett Foster, and got us inside.

I leaned in and whispered to Lane Davenport about the speakeasy hidden here during prohibition, and when he mentioned the tunnel, I snapped back with 'I know!'—then caught myself, realizing I couldn’t remember where it led.
I ran my hand over the wall, feeling the solid spots, then suddenly—there it was, a hollow thud under my palm, like a secret knocking back.
I turned to Lane Davenport and asked, 'Do you need volunteers?'—the words came out with a smile, but I already knew the answer.
I stepped forward and said I’d volunteer at Maplewood House—felt right, saying it out loud. Then I pulled Graham York along, not letting the moment drag.

I was just about to celebrate figuring out the tunnel’s dirt disposal when I rushed out and saw Graham York with Micah Davenport standing there — I froze, half-dressed, realizing I’d just spilled a crucial part of the plan to someone who wasn’t supposed to know.

I whispered to Graham York, 'You told her?' and felt the job start to unravel when he admitted it—telling Micah Davenport about the heist wasn't just stupid, it was a crime against the code. When he asked about bacon, all I could think to say was 'Crispy,' because nothing else in that kitchen made sense anymore.
I told Micah Davenport straight—'I'm a confidence man,' not a con man. It's about faith, belief, the Latin 'fides'—that's what I'm about, not just ripping people off.
I said it plain—I like Westhaven Theater. Three hots and a cot. For me, it's a win-win. Micah Davenport looked at me like I was crazy, but it's the truth.

I told Micah Davenport that Graham York would be perfect for Evan Hart because he’s not an actor—he’d be playing himself, a man from nothing who remade his life and loves her like Evan Hart loves Micah Davenport.
She looked at me like I’d moved the ground under her, then slapped me—hard—right across the face. I didn’t flinch. Just said, 'Fair enough.'
I moved the armoire aside with Graham York, no hesitation—just muscle and motion. The wall behind it was the only way forward, and we both knew it.
I laid one blanket on the floor to catch debris and held another against the wall to keep the noise down. Every hammer strike had to be buried—sound could bring everything crashing down.
I shone my flashlight into the tunnel and saw nothing but dust and empty space—then I went in first, stepping into the dark like it owed me something.
I saw a glint on the floor—trolley tracks. That meant someone had moved dirt through here before, maybe recently. The beam caught them just right as I swept the flashlight ahead.
We hit a soot-covered wall ten feet in. Graham York said we were twenty feet short and needed another pair of hands. I felt the weight of the brick—he was right, but I didn’t like it.
I looked Skyler Vaughn dead in the eye and laid it out — 'Are you in or are you in?' — and he didn't flinch, just picked up the shovel and started digging.
I said it out loud—Florida. Just the word felt like a crack of light in all this cold, like something warm could still exist.
I was eating cheerios and talking to Graham York about Micah Davenport when Shawn Vaughn walked in, said he was in, or I was out, and sat down like he belonged there.
Blair Sawyer leaned in and said he could give us the date, help with alarms, and be our guy inside.
He said his wife Annie died after the Westhaven Plaza wouldn't help with the bills, and I could hear the bitterness in his voice — like he'd been carrying that weight for years.
I told Graham York we couldn't wait for closing night—he has to leave her, no looking back. The rain was coming down, and he was hesitating, but this is the only shot we’ve got.
I burst out the back door of Maplewood House and started running—no hesitation, no look back. The job just changed, and I moved.
I stepped in front of that gun and told Skyler Vaughn to stay put—Shawn Vaughn could shoot me, but he’d have to do it right there. Then he punched me in the gut and cracked my head on the floor.
I got on top of Shawn Vaughn, slammed his head into the ground, and yelled in his face—some old rage just came out. Then I saw Graham York was bleeding on the leg.

I get this twitch! and then I give him my answer: "I'm gonna break in your house, set your dog on fire, eat all your food, go on a naked rampage through your garden, dance in the streets of your l'il hometown like a crazed harpee, hurl myself headlong flaming
Ah. Mistaken identity. A perennial favorite. Identities are just constructs, anyway. They're mistaken all the time.
Time is a medium of exchange. You can buy things with it. Education. Self-respect. You can even figure out your dream.
Because life ain't like that. There's always a cost. That's why they call it life. You got to pay somewhere. The piper
Don't forget. Your dream is your myth is your truth.

I never liked that word. It's only half
of what it is. The word confidence comes
from the latin. Fides. With Faith.
Belief.
But I was always much better at the feeling good part than the ripping off part. (THEN) Hence, the Westhaven Theater.
Your dream is your truth is your destiny.
Sleep is for the blessed.
Palm trees. Sandy beaches. All you can eat sunshine. Grapefruits as big as your head!
Your dream is your truth is your destiny!
This was your chance you idiot. You could've been a better man but you did it again. You messed up. And now you're back with the maggots. Just one big missed opportunity.
The only thing I've ever missed in twentythree years is a hot bath. And that ain't worth walking out of here for.

I can see it, Graham York. It's all in front of me. the small lantern. The Westhaven Plaza. The tunnel. The pieces of the puzzle are on the table. All we got to do is put them in the right order! The only thing is the dirt...where does the dirt from the tunnel go?
